newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks to cut export tax break to raise funds.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks to cut export tax break to raise funds.

text.p: President Bill Clinton wants to curtail a corporate tax break on export sales to help pay for his convention-week programmes, but past attempts to change the law have run into opposition in Congress.

As part of his triumphal march to the Democratic party convention in Chicago, Clinton has announced ways to promote literacy and protect the environment, and he was expected to unveil a plan to create jobs for people getting off welfare when he accepts the presidential nomination on Thursday.

To pay for the $8.5 billion hodgepodge of programmes and keep Clinton's hard-earned credentials as a federal deficit-cutter, the president has released a list of "offsets," or ways to raise the money.

The biggest revenue-raiser was a $5.3 billion plan to increase taxes on export sales. But other attempts to chip away at this part of the tax law, most recently in 1992 and 1994, have not done well in Congress.

"This proposal has been trotted out before and it was shot down by Democratic Congresses. I don't think it's going to be passed by a Republican-majority Congress," said J.D. Foster, executive director of the Washington-based Tax Foundation, a non-profit, non-partisan research and education organisation.
Opponents of the change, including multinational companies and trade associations, have set up the "Export Source Coalition" named after the corporate tax break the White House was attacking.
"We've had good bipartisan support in Congress," said Barbara Washburn, chairperson of the coalition. "We hope they will continue to see the importance of retaining the export source rule."

Current law allows all businesses to pay U.S. taxes on only 50 percent of their export income. It is based on the assumption that the exporter also pays taxes in the country where the product is sold, and might otherwise be taxed twice.
Any company, from a large multinational corporation to a mom-and-pop company selling computer software across the border to Canada, could benefit from the tax break.

The Clinton administration argued that it was too generous in some cases, and that the percentage of export profits taxed in the United States should be calculated where most of the "economic activity" to make the export took place.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce reacted sharply, declaring Clinton was "picking the pockets of American business."

"For the last four years it has been President clinton's approach to treat businesses as his political piggy bank. Unfortunately, this approach will have long-term negative implications for economic growth," Martin Regalia, the chamber's chief economist, said in a statement.

Clinton has already called for scaling back the export sales tax break last June as a way to pay for another proposal -- his idea to give families a $1500 tax credit for each child attending his or her first year of college.
Then, the administration proposed reducing from 50 to 25 percent the amount of export profits that could be considered foreign income and thus excluded from U.S. taxes.
Stan Collender, budget analyst at Price Waterhouse, said there was nothing wrong with the White House drawing on the same revenue-raiser in two different proposals.

"Everyone does that all the time, especially when the first thing has been rejected," he said. "It (the college tax credit) hasn't been taken up and the Republican Congress clearly has no plans to do so.
"If Clinton is re-elected and wants to spend the money both ways, well then he would have to come up with a way," Collender said.
